content: Moderate complexity automated nucleic acid amplification tests (NAATs) can be utilized on respiratory samples to detect pulmonary tuberculosis (TB) and resistance to rifampicin and isoniazid in individuals presenting with signs and symptoms of pulmonary TB. This approach is recommended over traditional culture and phenotypic drug susceptibility testing (DST), based on moderate certainty of evidence regarding diagnostic accuracy. Loop-mediated isothermal amplification (TB-LAMP) may serve as a replacement for sputum-smear microscopy in diagnosing pulmonary TB in adults with symptoms consistent with TB. This is a conditional recommendation supported by very low certainty evidence. TB-LAMP can also be used as a follow-up test to sputum-smear microscopy, particularly when further testing of smear-negative specimens is required. The Xpert MTB/RIF assay is a cartridge-based automated test that employs real-time polymerase chain reaction (PCR) on the GeneXpert® platform. It detects Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex and mutations associated with rifampicin resistance directly from sputum samples in under two hours. The Xpert MTB/RIF Ultra assay, an enhanced version, improves sensitivity and reliability for detecting M. tuberculosis complex and rifampicin resistance. Trace results are common in pediatric specimens due to the paucibacillary nature of TB in children. For children and individuals living with HIV being evaluated for pulmonary or extrapulmonary TB, an M. tuberculosis complex detected trace result is considered bacteriological confirmation of TB. The Truenat MTB and MTB Plus assays use chip-based real-time micro-PCR for semi-quantitative detection of M. tuberculosis complex directly from sputum samples, providing results in less than an hour. These assays are designed for use in peripheral laboratories with minimal infrastructure and training. If the result is positive, the extracted DNA can be further tested using the Truenat MTB-RIF Dx assay to detect rifampicin resistance mutations. The urine lateral flow lipoarabinomannan (LF-LAM) assay detects the mycobacterial lipoarabinomannan antigen in urine. It is particularly useful as a point-of-care test for individuals living with HIV, especially in urgent cases where rapid TB diagnosis is critical for survival. However, its sensitivity is limited. The Alere Determine TB LAM Ag is the only commercially available LF-LAM test endorsed by WHO. Routine HIV testing should be offered to all children and adolescents undergoing evaluation for TB exposure, presumptive TB, or confirmed TB diagnosis. Early detection of HIV infection is crucial for integrated management of TB/HIV co-infection. All children and adolescents with HIV-associated TB are eligible for antiretroviral therapy (ART) and co-trimoxazole prophylaxis. Chest X-ray (CXR) remains an important diagnostic tool for TB in children, particularly when bacteriological tests are negative or unavailable. Most children with pulmonary TB exhibit radiographic changes suggestive of TB. Abnormalities on CXR indicative of pulmonary TB include enlarged perihilar or paratracheal lymph nodes, dense alveolar opacification, miliary patterns, cavitation (more common in adolescents), and pleural or pericardial effusion. Adolescents with TB often present with radiographic changes similar to adults, such as apical infiltrates with or without cavity formation or unilateral large pleural effusions. Good-quality CXRs, including lateral views when possible, are essential for thorough clinical evaluation and should be interpreted by trained personnel. CXR findings are often nonspecific and cannot solely determine the correct treatment. However, they are useful in supporting clinical diagnosis when TB is suspected, especially in cases with negative bacteriological tests. CXRs can also help assess disease severity, determine eligibility for shorter treatment regimens, and evaluate treatment response. Testing for M. tuberculosis infection using tuberculin skin test (TST) or interferon-gamma release assays (IGRAs) can support TB diagnosis in children with suggestive clinical features who are sputum smear-negative or unable to produce sputum. A positive test indicates prior or current infection with M. tuberculosis. However, these tests do not distinguish between TB infection and active TB disease.
